title: JavaScript syntax — quick overview
rememberThis: JavaScript has Automatic Semicolon Insertion (ASI) — return on its own line before { } is a classic bug; C# errors on missing semicolons instead.
Default to const; use let when reassigning; avoid var in new code — var hoists to undefined, let/const hit TDZ before their line.
if ( ) accepts truthy/falsy — not bool-only like C#. Eight falsy: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN.
=== is strict equality like C# ==; avoid == coercion. ?? defaults null/undefined only; || defaults all falsy values.
for...of walks iterable values (C# foreach); for...in walks enumerable object keys — not for array elements.
switch uses === and falls through without break. Template literals use backticks and ${expr} — like C# $"{expr}".
bullets: TDZ: reading let/const before the declaration throws ReferenceError — not undefined like var.
Optional chaining ?. short-circuits to undefined; no ?. = assignment in JavaScript (C# 14 has x?.Prop = v).
Precedence trap: a ?? b || c parses as (a ?? b) || c — parenthesize mixed ??, ||, and ?:.
Empty array [] is truthy; empty string "" is falsy — top interview trick.
break and continue work in for/for...of/while — not inside Array.forEach callbacks.
Tagged templates: tag`text ${val}` calls tag(strings, ...values) for DSLs and sanitizers.
